title: Routing Ownership and Fencing Patterns
body:
Purpose
-----
Working notes to clarify who owns routing decisions and fencing for the three serving modes (Hosted, Dedicated, Private). This is a practical playbook for engineers and on-call to use when designing new tenant attachment models or triaging cross-tenant leaks or noisy-tenant incidents.

Context and motivation
----------------------
We frequently get ambiguous boundaries between network/control responsibilities: e.g., a misconfigured canary in Dedicated spilling KV-cache keys to shared LBs, or Private customers expecting full control over egress routing while still wanting Redwood visibility for billing. This doc frames patterns that map operational ownership to technical controls. Focus: routing ownership, failure isolation, control-plane role separation, multi-region considerations.

High-level pattern summary
--------------------------
- Ownership model: assign one of three owners to each routing function: Platform (Redwood control plane), Tenant (customer-managed), or Hybrid (shared responsibility).
- Fencing primitives: Network-level (VPC, NSGs), Process-level (per-tenant runtime processes or cgroups), Cache/State-level (prefix scoping + key namespaces), and Policy-level (ingress/egress ACLs).
- Failure domains: map routing handoffs to explicit failure domains: control-plane, data-plane, and infra-plane.

Matrix: Hosted / Dedicated / Private (high-level)
------------------------------------------------
Hosted:
- Routing ownership: Platform. Global front-door, region-aware edge routing, automatic fallback to lower-cost variants.
- Fencing: Logical tenant IDs + prefix-scoped caches, strict routing policies in edge layer, tenant rate-limiting enforced at API gateway.
- Control-plane boundaries: single Redwood control plane manages routing decisions. Customers cannot change routing policies except via pre-approved config options (model pinning, region hints).
- Multi-region: Active-active with platform-controlled geo-affinity.

Dedicated:
- Routing ownership: Hybrid. Tenant gets reserved capacity but platform still owns front-door and multi-region failover.
- Fencing: Compute isolation via reserved pools; stronger network isolation optional (dedicated VPC peering) but often not by default. Cache fencing must be explicit: recommend per-tenant cache partitions rather than shared caches on the same node.
- Control-plane boundaries: Redwood retains routing policy for failover; tenant can request local-only routing via SRE runbooks.
- Multi-region: Customer can select primary region; platform provides automated DR and cross-region spillover with explicit notification windows.

Private (VPC / On-prem):
- Routing ownership: Tenant-first. Customer owns ingress/egress control plane; Redwood provides a light control-plane agent for telemetry and rollout coordination.
- Fencing: Full network isolation typically enforced; default install should enable strict tenant-only routing at the edge.
- Control-plane boundaries: Control-plane agent accepts signed policy bundles from Redwood but tenant can override at install time.
- Multi-region: Subject to customer topology; platform provides best-effort cross-site tooling but not automatic failover unless contractually agreed.

Operational patterns and recommendations
---------------------------------------
1) Explicit ownership tags on every routing rule: add metadata {owner: platform|tenant|hybrid, failover: allow|deny, sla-tier: gold|silver|bronze}. This is simple YAML in route config and surfaces in dashboards and change reviews.

2) Cache fencing: avoid colocating multiple tenant caches in a single LRU instance unless using namespace-anchored eviction. Default: allocate logical KV namespaces per tenant; if physical colocation is used, enable per-tenant quotas and eviction isolation.

3) Circuit-breaker placement: put token-level circuit breakers at the gateway for Hosted; in Dedicated place breakers at the reserved pool ingress; in Private document recommended locations and provide a sample eBPF filter for on-prem.

4) Canary and rollout constraints: canaries originating in platform should never run on Private customer node pools; for Dedicated count canaries as tenant-scoped unless explicitly requested. Prevent cross-tenant tool calls during rollout by default.

5) Multi-region affinity and sticky routing: use region hints and locality heuristics, but always preserve explicit tenant-level override in Dedicated and Private. For Hosted default to latency-first.

Edge cases and incident notes
----------------------------
- Noisy-tenant spillover: if noisy tenant saturates shared egress in Dedicated, route new requests to burst capacity pool or trigger tenant throttling. SRE runbook: PLAT-427 outlines throttles + customer notification.
- Control-plane unavailability: Hosted falls back to precomputed routing tables; Dedicated falls back to local pool-level defaults; Private must have local fallback config or accept degraded mode.

Sample routing policy snippet (informal)
--------------------------------------
- route: /v1/generate
  owner: platform
  allow_fallback: true
  cache_namespace: tenant-${TENANT_ID}
  max_tokens_per_minute: 10000  # per-tenant

Design tradeoffs called out
--------------------------
- Platform-owned routing gives better SLOs and easier global failover but increases trust requirements for customers.
- Tenant-owned routing reduces blast radius for platform changes but increases operational burden on customers and reduces global optimization opportunities (e.g., cheapest region selection).
- Hybrid models are complex but often necessary for Dedicated: they require clear change windows and explicit escalation paths.

Open questions and work items
----------------------------
- Define exact metadata schema for route ownership and enforce via linting in the route config PR check. (owner: platform|tenant|hybrid; sensitive: true|false; region_affinity: soft|hard).
- Implement per-tenant cache namespaces in the runtime and add an opt-in physical partitioning mode for heavy tenants.
- Build dashboard panels that surface route owner and last-change author to aid incident response.

Next steps (short horizon)
-------------------------
- (0-2w) Add route metadata lint rule and gating. Assignee: Benji.
- (2-6w) Prototype per-tenant cache namespace support in serving-runtime; run perf tests for heavy-tenancy churn. Assignee: Mikael.
- (4-8w) Draft customer-facing guidance for Dedicated deployments that explains routing tradeoffs and recommended defaults. Assignee: Lena.

Notes to reviewers
------------------
This is a working draft: please add examples from recent incidents, call out missing escalation paths, and add links to any Dedicated contract language that mandates specific routing behavior. Prefer concrete runbook references over abstract statements.
